subsubtopic: CALL FOR REFERRAL TO PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to protest the arrogant manner in which the metric conversion program is being forced on the Canadian consumer. The Metric Commission's own internal Gallup poll, which has been suppressed, clearly shows that a majority of Canadians polled are against metric. To add insult to injury the government is now, by order in council, giving another $3 million to the commission in addition to the $49.3 million already spent. Enough is enough. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga):
That the entire matter of metric conversion be referred to the appropriate committee of this House so that members and witnesses from the public sector may have the right to challenge the legality and necessity of metric conversion in Canada.

That the Minister of Transport now adopt a serious and Canada-First posture on this debacle and honour forthwith his government's previous commitment that duty-free shops would be operated by Canadian-owned enterprises.

That this House urges the minister responsible for the status of women, in making further appointments to the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women, to overcome that Liberal propensity which leads her to ignore women in the labour force, low-income women and native women.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I too rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. On Monday, Mayor Charles Royer of Seattle came to Vancouver to publicize a combination of gifts and threats in a stepped-up effort to persuade British Columbians to accept the inundation of 5,000 acres of prime recreational land in the Skagit Valley. That the government take immediate action to appoint a Canadian chairman to the commission, that the IJC hold full public hearings on the Skagit Valley issue and that the federal government make a detailed presentation at these hearings emphasizing the environmental devastation which will take place if flooding is permitted.

subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF NATIVE PEOPLE IN NORTHEASTERN ALBERTA-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, while the unemployment rate across Canada has reached the unprecedented level of 9 per cent, the Indians in my riding of Athabasca are experiencing unemployment rates of up to 80 per cent and 90 per cent. The people of the Bigstone Band, the Janvier Band, the Fort Chipewyan Band, the Cold Lake Band, the Fort MacKay Band, the Fort McMurray Band, the Sucker Creek Band, and many, many others continue to live in abject poverty, a situation which is getting progressively worse. Whereas the economic development which has come to this area has passed native peoples by and continues to leave them
far behind, I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga):
That the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development be directed by this House to earmark funds for economic development to allow the native people of northeastern Alberta to participate in and benefit from the economic activity taking place instead of leaving them behind in poverty and despair.

subsubtopic: POLLUTION OF NIAGARA RIVER-CALL FOR REFERRAL TO PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Last week I and a number of my colleagues in the NDP caucus investigated charges from citizen and environmental groups that the Niagara River is being severely polluted by the chemical industry which is discharging waste materials into the river, and we determined that there is every reason for concern, despite the protestations from the Minister of the Environment to the contrary. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton):
That this House directs the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry to establish an all-party subcommittee on persistent toxic substances to investigate the charges of citizen, scientific, legal and environmental groups that the dumping of toxic chemical wastes into the Niagara River is posing a serious hazard to this important water source, to fisheries, and to the health of Canadians.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Thousands of Canadians who borrow money to purchase registered retirement savings plans are very concerned, because the minister proposed in the budget that interest on such loans should not be tax deductible. However, since the budget has under-

February 17, 1982
Oral Questions
gone a number of changes, several of my constituents now wonder whether this particular measure might be changed as well.
My question is as follows: Does the minister intend to remove their cause for concern and allow Canadians to continue to deduct that interest from their income tax?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: DEDUCTIBILITY OF INTEREST ON LOANS USED FOR PURCHASE OF REGISTERED RETIREMENT SAVINGS PLANS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: No, Madam Speaker, it is not my intention to propose any further changes at this stage.

subtopic: PROVISIONS AFFECTING HEALTH AND INSURANCE PLANS
PROVISIONS AFFECTING HEALTH AND INSURANCE PLANS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same minister. The minister is aware that there is widespread uncertainty across Canada about payroll deductions with respect to dental and health insurance plans. Some employees are now paying taxes through payroll deductions, and some employers have not yet begun to make deductions. Because of the prevailing confusion will the minister tell us whether or not he is contemplating further changes to the budget in this area?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: PROVISIONS AFFECTING HEALTH AND INSURANCE PLANS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think I should clarify the situation for the benefit of the hon. member. Quite a number of representations were made following the budget in November and December. As the hon. member knows, on December 18 I made a number of changes which I regarded as necessary and urgent. It is my view that any further changes based upon representations and arguments of hon. members ought to be made when we reach the appropriate stage of the legislative process.

Madam Speaker, my final supplementary question is directed to the same minister. Many small business people and farmers sold their farms before November 12, fully intending to buy IAACs before February 28, 1982, as the minister is aware. The minister's various statements, including the one of yesterday, ignored the retroactive impact of the budget in this regard with respect to small business people and farmers. Therefore, will he remove this retroactive feature of the budget by extending the date on which income averaging rules are to be changed, to February 28, 1982?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the hon. member knows, where written agreements were in effect prior to the budget, of course these arrangements can proceed. In addition, it is possible for individuals in that particular case to purchase a one-year IAAC and next year to transfer the proceeds from that purchase into a forward-averaging system. It seems to me that these provisions have met the main difficulties and the main concerns. Naturally I am quite prepared, when we go to
committee, to hear the views of hon. members on that and on any other subject.
When will that be?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: As soon as possible.

subsubtopic: SINKING OF "OCEAN RANGER" DRILLING RIG-QUERY RESPECTING STANDBY VESSEL
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who has sort of pre-empted the issue of the Ocean Ranger. The three inspection reports tabled yesterday referred to supply boats and standby vessels. I should like to ask the minister whether there was a standby vessel in the vicinity of the Ocean Ranger. If so, how close was it to the Ocean Ranger? Was there a signal to the standby boat? If not, why not, especially in view of the stringent regulations of Norway after the Norwegian disaster in the North Sea, whereby emergency standby boats are required under the rules and regulations of the Norway government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: SINKING OF "OCEAN RANGER" DRILLING RIG-QUERY RESPECTING STANDBY VESSEL
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have been informed that there was at least one standby boat. There may have been more; 1 believe there were two. With respect to the other questions asked by the hon. member, as to whether a signal was sent and what not, I shall inquire and be happy to report to him.

Madam Speaker, when the minister is checking that rather basic fact, would he also check to see if whatever regulations we were following for the Ocean Ranger in Canadian waters required that each person on the rig have a survival suit? In the inspection report this was mentioned for the helicopter crew. Could the minister in his reply tell us just what specifications and regulations we do follow for oil rigs in Canadian waters? Are they American regulations, the more stringent Norwegian ones, or do we have any regulations?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Madam Speaker, first of all the hon. member should note that the Ocean Ranger was not in Canadian waters. It was stationed in international waters. The regulations concerning oil and gas drilling are in print and public. They cover operations offshore. As I indicated in the House yesterday, Section 8 of the regulations elaborates on all the information required to be furnished by operators, with regard to drilling programs.

On the safety of a rig?
February 17, 1982

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: He will find numerous provisions and requirements that he cannot expect me to read into the record during question period. 1 will be happy to give the hon. member a copy of the oil and gas drilling regulations if he does not have them already.
On safety of rigs?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Yes, on safety. There are all kinds of provisions. There are some on support craft and standby craft. There are some provisions concerning anchors, stability of a unit, and on and on. I suggest to the hon. member that he refer to the regulations. With regard to very detailed questions as to the operations and exactly what happened on the platform at a particular time, I have to tell the hon. member right away that 1 am not in a position to give him that information. We have set up a commission of inquiry under the chairmanship of the Chief Justice of Newfoundland. We expect during the course of the inquiry that all those facts will be fully investigated and all the relevant information will be made available. But I am not in a position, and I do not think the hon. member would expect me to be in a position, to give the type of detail that he is asking for today. 1 am taking notice of his request and if I can provide the hon. member with additional information I will be very happy to do so.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO CONTROL MORTGAGE INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Finance has indicated on numerous occasions, both in the House and to me personally, that he believed the mortgage interest rates currently being charged in this country are too high. He has further stated that the banks should bleed a little and that he would monitor profits. We now see the banks are again leading the way toward even higher interest rates.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO CONTROL MORTGAGE INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Some bleeding.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO CONTROL MORTGAGE INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Traditionally the difference between the consumer price index and the mortgage interest rate charged has been approximately three points, that is from 1970 to 1981. The banks now claim they need a four to six-point spread. Their spread right now is between five and seven points. Today's announcement of even higher interest rates will take that spread up to nine-plus points between the consumer price index and the mortgage interest rate charged on the some
250,000	mortgage renewals that will take place this year.
Will the minister bring in legislation now that will establish a mortgage interest rate that Canadians can afford?
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO CONTROL MORTGAGE INTEREST RATES
speechtext: You voted against that.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION TO CONTROL MORTGAGE INTEREST RATES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if it were possible to do it that easily, I assure my hon. friend I would be the first to agree to an easy proposal of that kind. I do not think it is possible in these circumstances simply to bring in a bill establishing a particular rate and expect the necessary funds to flow in at a non-competitive rate or one which is not related to the market. The hon. member knows that, and that is why, when a similar proposal was put forward by the opposition in a non-confidence motion, we voted against it. The effect of supporting it would really be to deny individuals necessary funds at the market rate.
The hon. member has raised the question of the performance of banks, and so on. I have already agreed that it would be useful for members of this House to examine the question of bank profits, and I am quite prepared to have that done when hon. members are ready to pass the reference and get the committee in operation.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER GIVE DIRECTION TO BANKS
REQUEST THAT MINISTER GIVE DIRECTION TO BANKS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is incredible how the minister can dismiss the needs of so many Canadians when it comes to the question of finding affordable housing. To say it is difficult to bring in legislation establishing a mortgage ceiling is to deny that people are entitled to affordable accommodation. I put to the minister, notwithstanding any inquiry we might have, it is quite clear on the record that bank profits have gone up from $672 million in 1977 to $ 1.6 billion in 1981.
Now, by anyone's admission there are two irrefutable facts. One, we need housing for people at a price they can afford, and we are falling short by some 70,000 units this year alone; and, two, we have unemployed people who could build those houses. Will the minister not undertake to direct that the banks not only accept a mortgage interest rate ceiling that people can afford, but that they put a significant percentage of their investment capital into mortgages in order that we can create the housing that people need, and create jobs for those currently unemployed?

subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER GIVE DIRECTION TO BANKS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER GIVE DIRECTION TO BANKS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, there is nothing 1 can add to my earlier answer. I believe it would be useful at this stage, in view of the reference once again by the hon. member to bank profits, to have the matter fully investigated by a parliamentary committee. If that committee can provide recommendations to me on that subject, then I would consider them very seriously. Up to the present I have stated to the House that the reason in my view it is not appropriate at this stage to move on the tax side is because such a move would

February 17, 1982
Oral Questions
deny to many borrowers in the community the tax advantages they enjoy from the banks.
Because of existing arrangements, if we put a tax on the banks we would indeed deny a large number of borrowers access to money at much lower rates of interest. That is the reason I have not proposed a tax on the banks as I have been asked to do. I believe it would be self-defeating. If hon. members want to study the matter and can come up with a better answer, then I would be glad to consider it.

I am sure the minister appreciates that if there is to be a study, surely it must be initiated by the government and not by the opposition. I ask the minister to consider that there are two factors in life which are absolutely essential: food and shelter. How can the minister claim it is outside his jurisdiction and power to direct banks and all other financial institutions with regard to interest rates and the amount of their investment capital which must go into affordable housing? I simply ask the minister does the government have no sense of responsibility to ensure that people in Canada can get accommodation at a price they can afford, and to ensure that banks do not gouge the public in the way they have?
Hear, hear!
Why do you support them?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, it was in this particular session of the House of Commons, of the Parliament of Canada-
Only had one!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: -that the decennial revision of the Bank Act was undertaken.
We tried to get it at fixed interest rates.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: The House of Commons established the rules and regulations governing the banking system, including the possibility of foreign banks coming into Canada in order to increase the competitive character of the banking system. There is no provision in the law which permits the Minister of Finance to establish the rates at which banks-
We'll put it in.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: -either borrow or lend money. That ought to be clear to the hon. member.
We will put it in!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The hon. member has rightly concentrated attention on the problem of home owners. As he knows, we have provided a system by which we believe no home owner in
this country will lose a home because of high interest rates. We have appealed to the banks, for example, to roll back some of the interest rate increases last summer. One of the major banks did that with considerable benefit to potential home owners. Other banks would have my support if they undertook similar activity. However, there is no power within the hands of the Minister of Finance to direct the banks as to how to conduct their day to day operations, much as-
We will give you the power.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: -at times, I might like to do so.

subsubtopic: TAX MEASURE AFFECTING LIFE INSURANCE POLICIES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of Finance. On November 12 the Minister of Finance announced a tax on whole life insurance policies, making Canada the only country in the western world to do so. Since then the minister said he may refer the matter to committee, he may make arrangements with the insurance companies, or he may do nothing. This has caused a great deal of uncertainty, both for the sellers and purchasers of whole life insurance. Will the minister now take the proper course and announce that he is abandoning this foolish tax measure and end the uncertainty?

subsubtopic: TAX MEASURE AFFECTING LIFE INSURANCE POLICIES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: TAX MEASURE AFFECTING LIFE INSURANCE POLICIES
speechtext: No, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, did the minister know when he introduced his infamous budget on the night of November 12 that 78 per cent of all those who own whole life insurance policies earn under $25,000? That is what the average Canadian earns. How, in the name of equity, could he say that this was a budget which was taxing the rich when the average Canadian is paying tax on his life insurance, while deputy ministers earning $80,000 a year get a $4,500 tax break? subsubtopic: DEATH OF DR. JIR1 SKVOR
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I cannot comment on that visit. I do not know whether it took place or who attended it. subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW RELATING TO CERTAIN TAXES AND TO PROVIDE OTHER AUTHORITY FOR THE RAISING OF FUNDS MEASURE TO AMEND

speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, February 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bussieres that Bill C-93, to amend the statute law relating to certain taxes and to provide other authority for the raising of funds, be read the second time and referred to Committee of the Whole.

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW RELATING TO CERTAIN TAXES AND TO PROVIDE OTHER AUTHORITY FOR THE RAISING OF FUNDS MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as you are aware, Bill C-93 is another attempt by the government to dupe Canadian citizens out of billions of dollars. This time it is $6.6 billion. Last time it was $14 billion. All of that money is to be borrowed.
I stand as a member of the opposition but also as a member who represents citizens who have had enough of this growth of government and who are opposing this wholesale borrowing of money. This money is to be raised in any currency. This means that the government can borrow from any country in the world. This would only exacerbate the problem we already have with our balance of trade. It means that more money will leave this country than comes in. The government can give any form of security that it wants-it could put a mortgage on your house, Mr. Speaker, on my house, and it is certainly putting a mortgage on our future. Therefore, I have no difficulty at all in opposing this bill.
It is clear that we have a government that is totally out of control, and that has been the case since it was returned. I should like to go through the remarks made by the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) which show that the government has no idea how to run an economy. Our economy is being run by a bunch of people who have never had to meet a payroll and who have never seen the tragedy of people losing their jobs as a result of government inflation.
The minister proudly referred to the fact that the government had signed agreements with Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia. He was trying to gather some credit for the government as if all the energy taxes, because they were part of an agreement, somehow gave the federal government legitimacy. That argument will not hold, Mr. Speaker. In fact, what the producing provinces did under the agreement was to get a confirmation that they simply had rights as owners of the assets; all they were putting into the agreement was their right as owners. All of the other taxes that have been imposed upon Canadians and that are in the process of being imposed upon them, are the result of decisions made by the Liberal Party of this country.
We must keep in mind that when a gallon of gas sells in Ontario for $1.67, some 22 cents of that goes to the citizens of Alberta as owners; some 25 cents goes to the Ontario government as a provincial tax it has chosen to levy on its own people, and some 57 cents goes to the federal government by way of a simple tax. It is not necessary for the federal government to raise money that way. There is income tax and sales tax, but rather than increase the income tax, the federal government has chosen to impose this tax on energy. It is another way for the federal government to raise money. Some 63 cents out of that $1.67 goes to the companies, most of which are Canadian, that explore for the oil, that drill for the oil, that will produce it, and then refine it. All of the distribution system, all of the wholesalers and retailers-that huge package of Canadians- shares some 63 cents.
The price of energy is much higher than it needs to be in this country, and the reason for this is taxation by governments and primarily by the government opposite. We must always remember that, Mr. Speaker. The minister said that in the perspective of the government, inflation is the number one problem. It is true that inflation is a serious matter; no one
February 17, 1982

denies that. He said that inflation forces interest rates up and slows investment, and that it must stop. He is absolutely correct, but he never said that there are three strings to the bow of this problem.
The first string is the deficit which the government will not admit it is responsible for. The deficit is over $90 billion. One dollar in five of our revenue goes to service that debt, so the government has lost the flexibility of being able to step in and help other parts of the industry when they need help. It is unable to help citizens who are losing their farms and ranches. But the one dollar in five of federal revenue that services the debt goes into the hands of people who already have wealth. Those are the people in our country and in other countries who have wealth. That is a very bad thing, because it leads to a class society.
So the first string, Mr. Speaker, is the deficit, and it is the one that the government will not admit to-it is too many dollars chasing the available goods that causes inflation. People have the money and they put out more on goods than they need to, and that causes inflation. As a result of inflation we have high interest rates, in order to try to bring it down.
The government says that we need high interest rates to bring inflation down but in truth, Mr. Speaker, the way to bring inflation down quickly and permanently is to get the size of government itself under control, and particularly the government deficit.
From the last financial statement we know that the government has some $7 billion on deposit with the chartered banks today. Yet it comes before us, as elected members responsible to our constituents across the country, and asks permission to borrow an additional $6.6 billion. I do not believe that we should give the cabinet that authority. I believe that the government backbenchers, in response to their own citizens, should deny the government access to this money. It simply does not need it when it already has $7 billion in the till. When that money is gone it can come back to the House when it genuinely needs more and ask for it. If the government takes that $6.6 out of the economy tomorrow, that means it is not available to the private companies and the ordinary citizens who may need it to build the plant and manufacturing capacity that will put Canadians to work. When that $6.6 billion is drawn from the capital market, it is just not available.
The government should not be able to do that to people, and that is why I believe that we need a constitutional amendment to block governments from having deficits. West Germany has this in its constitution. Governments should only be able to go into a deficit situation if there is an emergency or a crisis. Such a provision should be part of our Constitution in order to protect the citizens against the government.

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW RELATING TO CERTAIN TAXES AND TO PROVIDE OTHER AUTHORITY FOR THE RAISING OF FUNDS MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: We have a crisis right now.

subtopic: AN ACT TO AMEND THE STATUTE LAW RELATING TO CERTAIN TAXES AND TO PROVIDE OTHER AUTHORITY FOR THE RAISING OF FUNDS MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Yesterday the Minister of State for Finance talked glowingly about how the government was restraining itself. 1 believe he is a man of some honour and reputation, a
Taxation
man with a sound educational background, but surely he must find that statement incredible in these tough times when every citizen has to cut back and tighten his belt. On the basis of the public accounts as well as the national accounts, government expenditures are rising 22 per cent. How can he possibly say that this amounts to restraint? If he could parallel this with a rate of inflation of only 11 per cent or 12 per cent, perhaps he' could say that it was restraint. But surely increasing government expenditures at twice the rate of inflation must be extravagant and are not restraint.
It is regrettable that history repeats itself. In 1974 when the Anti-Inflation Board was established, the government said to Canadians and to corporations that there had to be restraint. Thus, AIB held down wages of ordinary Canadian workers and held down prices to a lesser extent. Surely the third string in the bull had to be government holding itself down, but it did not. When we look at the record of the AIB we find that government expenditures rose enormously, and finally the controls had to come off. Canadians realized they were tricked, and they are being tricked again. Liberal members made campaign promises to hold down the price of energy and to be a sound government, but the Liberal government got us into deep trouble. Now we are at the point where the government is saying that we must hold back and tighten our belts, but once again it is not holding itself down. The whole system will not work. I say without a shadow of doubt that there will be enormous increases in inflation and high interest rates for many months, because the third string in the bull is not prepared to get itself under control.
Also the minister of state pointed out that all western nations were suffering from inflation. This is true, but most of them are suffering because they have had similar types of social democratic governments which have taken ordinary citizens into deficit positions. They are doing, as nations, what no one can do as an individual. None of us can spend more than we make and survive for more than a few weeks, months or years at the very most. Governments are no different. It is just that the time-frame before they are called to account is much longer, but the pain is always the same. If as an individual I spend more than I make, I am pushed into bankruptcy by my creditors, I declare bankruptcy and I suffer. When nations go into bankruptcy, people suffer. We can always predict who it will be-it will be people on fixed incomes because invariably governments get out of deficits by turning on the printing press. Every Canadian across the country needs to watch the weekly statement of the Bank of Canada. When the printing press is turned on, the nation is flooded with money. It is true that they will be paying back the deficit with 25-cent or 50-cent dollars, but who will suffer? It will be senior citizens on fixed incomes because they have no way of protecting themselves, and all people on welfare today will never get off the rolls. Now it is affecting middle-income Canadians, to the point where one must earn over $50,000 per year to purchase even a modest two-bedroom home.
What kind of a future is this for young people? Why should the government be able to get away with it? The answer is that

February 17, 1982
Taxation
the government should not get away with it, but it will continue to do so until people realize and vote in governments committed to financial restraint and prepared to bring forward a constitutional amendment which, as a matter of law, the supreme law of the land, prevents governments from doing such things.
Another argument used by the government is that tax rates for some 12 million Canadians will drop. All of this has been exposed for what it really is-a joke and a lie. In order to benefit these 12 million people, the government had to bring in an indexation clause. Because of the indexing, which is part of our law, the government is taking credit for 12 million people receiving a benefit. This is a lie because indexing is part of the law, and the government should not take credit for it any more than it should take credit for personal exemptions.
I suppose the government could say that 14 million Canadians are receiving a tax reduction because of personal exemptions, but it does not make sense. It is technically true that part of the budget will result in a reduction for some Canadians, but we must realize that it is a trick because on 11 separate occasions the government filed Ways and Means motions imposing taxes upon Canadians. I should like to refer to the various notices of Ways and Means motions that have been filed by the government. On Monday, April 21, 1980, a number of Ways and Means motions were filed; on July 11, 1980, the text of a Ways and Means motion was filed; on October 28, 1980, another notice was filed; on December 17,
1980,	another was filed; on Thursday, December 18 and on Friday, December 19, 1980, a separate taxing bill was filed; on March 2, 1981, a notice of taxation was filed; and on April 23,
1981,	another notice of taxation. These are all notices to impose taxes on Canadian citizens. For the government to stand and say that it reduced taxes on November 12 or December 18 is simply a lie. There was another notice of Ways and Means on June 2, 1981; one on November 12; one on November 27; and one as late as February 1, 1982. There were 11 separate occasions upon which the government imposed taxes on Canadian citizens. In total, 21 notices were filed. For the government to say that it reduced taxes in one provision might be technically correct, but in terms of honesty, equity and fairness to Canadians it is not true.
Why is Canada failing? It is a good question. We can look at our land and see some 24 million people sitting on resources spread across half the continent. We can look at our competitors, Japan and Germany. How would Mr. Speaker like to be one of 114 million Japanese sitting on a rock in the middle of the ocean, with no oil or resources? Its industry is its people. It has a low rate of inflation because the people work, and it has good productivity. It has the benefit of decent, honest government which does not try to fool the people. When we look at Germany, we see the same situation. Germany has a constitutional provision that the government cannot bring the people into a deficit position unless there is an emergency such as war.
Here we are in Canada with a government which is taking us into debt. It is the same situation with Crown corporations.
I had a paper prepared by the research department of the Library of Parliament which pointed out all our Crown corporations in Schedule C and Schedule D. Then it listed the subsidiary corporations owned by Crown corporations, and even the subsubsidiary corporations. Government involvement in our lives by virtue of Crown corporations is truly enormous. Indeed, the Liberal way to socialism in Canada is through Crown corporations. Fortunately, Canadians-and particularly university students-are beginning to realize that their futures are bankrupt. A deficit means that those of us who are middle aged will not have to pay the debt, but the next generation will be saddled with a deficit of over $90 billion. This has to be paid back out of the sweat and work of human beings, such as young people who work on oil rigs. It was a tragedy to lose 84 people off the Newfoundland coast. Every year in the western provinces there are 19 or 20 fatal accidents among oil rig workers. These lives are lost at the expense of providing oil for the rest of the country. That is the cost of operating oil rigs. They are very dangerous machines. What about those accidents involving crushed feet and other horrendous things? What about the miners who get black lung disease? All of these people are paying for the deficit. They work by the sweat of their brow. You would think that we would let them decide how to spend their money. But that is not the socialist way. The socialist way is for a government to take away all the money from the individual and decide how it will be spent rather than leave it to the individual to decide. The major difference that is now so clear to many Canadians is the difference between the Liberal-NDP style and our style. We would leave money with millions and millions of individuals and allow them to decide what to do with it. We believe this method leads to a better result for the nation than taxing money away from them and a small group of 36 cabinet ministers and deputy ministers deciding how to spend it.
The next budget will involve some $75 billion or $76 billion. That is about $2 billion for each cabinet minister. That is an incredible amount to me. I have a great suspicion of government. I would not want to see either a Conservative, an NDP or a Liberal government given that kind of power over us. Whenever power concentrates, power corrupts. It is not some pet phrase that power corrupts and absolute power corrupts absolutely. That is the experience of civilizations that have come and gone in the past. That is wisdom that has come to us through the passage of time. To the extent that we permit socialism to concentrate power in the hands of a Liberal government, an NDP government or a Conservative government, it matters not. We will have to fight the American Revolution again, and we will have to go back to the year 1215. see that during the 1950s and the 1960s Canada was doing well. The country was growing at an enormous rate each year vis-a-vis other countries in the world. Canada's standard of living was the second highest in the world. We were the envy of the world. One man told me he had come to this country and worked for 20 years building up about a half a million dollar livestock business. He is married and has five children. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me a good deal of pleasure to speak on Bill C-93. I wanted to say, first of all, that we as a nation are inordinately blessed with all sorts of riches, but we have not yet learned how to manage
Taxation
those riches appropriately. I wanted to indicate that in order to overcome our economic ills, we must surely deal with inflation. With inadequate productivity, with technological redundancy and inadequate inadequacy, with regional disparity and government debt and expenditure, the question is how and at what intensity or rate we should deal with inflation.
Today I want to try to be constructive, if I can. I want to say that I am in agreement that reducing inflation is the first priority, and that Canada's interest rate structure must, of necessity, closely follow that of our massive trading partner, the United States of America, on the short term, particularly so until we increase our relative productivity. Nevertheless, I am also convinced that Canada is rapidly approaching the bottom of the recessive cycle and that it is perhaps timely to give serious consideration to a program of selective stimulation of the economy, particularly with the prime objective of job creation.
1 believe we must minimize the length of the recession and accelerate the recovery period in any way we can, and we must start pretty soon. However, any regime of selective stimulation of the economy must unreservedly meet at least two conditions on the short term and perhaps on the longer-term basis. The first condition is that any program of selective economic stimulation must be non-inflationary. Some people may have difficulty envisioning programs of this sort; but there are many which can be implemented. The second condition must surely be that such programs must not increase government debt and direct government involvement in the economy through massive public borrowings.
These two conditions are important to be met with regard to any program of selective economic stimulation undertaken at the earliest opportunity. The question is, can it be done? If one anticipates substantive economic recovery in the next two or three years and government debt and expenditures can be held in check, then a basic selective tax policy, using future government tax revenues as an incentive to selectively stimulate the economy today, is an appropriate direction in which to move. The question is, how can it be done? Some of the long-term revenues of government should be used to selectively stimulate the economy today.
Let us examine the construction industry, and particularly the housing sector. Concerning the general industrial and commercial construction industry, surely rapid capital recovery or turnover in this high interest rate climate would be a substantial incentive. Why should the government not give very serious consideration to initiating a rapid, five-year regime or variable capital write-off regime for new construction during the next five years? Such a policy could start at the lower rate of depreciation or write-off in the first year and accelerate by 5 per cent a year to something like a very high rate in the fifth year, permitting capital recovery over a five-year period. This would be for new construction only. This would permit rapid capital recovery for reinvestment but, as it would only apply to new construction, increased construction would tend to increase government revenues rather than decrease them. The construction industry is so depressed today

that inflation would hardly be stimulated by such a program. Surely, a more generous and flexible use of the capital cost allowance, principle or incentive is timely today.
Let me look briefly at the housing industry. I have in my hand the report, I believe, of the last federal-provincial ministers conference on housing, which was held in Edmonton from January 31, 1978, to February 1, 1978, and jointly chaired by the current hon. Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) and myself. It is an interesting document, and most people should read it today because the predictions are quite accurate.
If governments wish to stimulate the housing construction in today's high interest rate climate, what type of housing should be stimulated? I think that is a very basic question. Should it be done? Should it be social housing? Should it be middle-income housing or should it be high-income housing? How should it be done, and with what incentives?
If job creation is to be the paramount objective, then it must be done without increasing inflation or government outlays. I believe this can be done through the construction of middle and high-income housing rather than low-income or social housing. I will explain this in more detail as I go along.
To build a one-bedroom suite or a senior citizens suite today, under the various government programs, be they federal or provincial, requires some $40,000 to $50,000. To service such a suite economically, with interest rates at 18.5 per cent, and considering taxes and capital recovery, the cost is approximately $10,000 a year, or just under $1,000 a month. Government subsidies for this type of housing vary in one form or another, but they run between 50 per cent and 60 per cent, so that a subsidy for all such housing would be in the order of $6,000 a year supplied by one or another level of government. Building an additional 100,000 units over a period of two years, for example, would involve subsidies by governments amounting to a minimum of $.5 billion.
Some people say "good" when the debt structure of the government, particularly the federal government, is what it is today. If one wanted to increase inflation through government borrowing, one would move rapidly and massively into the area of constructing social housing. However, if the priority were job creation and at the same time minimizing government debt and government involvement in the economy through government debt, what would one do?
First, let me say that our occupancy rate has fallen below three people per dwelling in most locations across this nation. Our housing stock is vastly underutilized. It is related to a period in our growth when we could afford a substantial amount of luxury. What is vitally necessary today are policies and programs to increase the utilization of existing Canadian housing stock.
A partition suite or a basement suite can readily be built today in the order of $4,000 to $5,000 as compared to new suites at $40,000 to $50,000 per unit. Why not allow home owners to partition houses and build basement units? This was
a great consideration of the housing ministers across the nation.
Why is it that existing housing stock is so inadequately used? Primarily this is because of municipal government regulation. I am certain that senior levels of government could meet with municipalities at the earliest opportunity to change bylaws and provide additional accommodation by way of more adequate use of existing housing, building basement suites or dividing homes in such a way that the vacancy rates of most of our urban centres would rapidly be increased. We should look seriously at moving in this direction at the earliest opportunity.
Just imagine the energy savings involved. Imagine the savings in reductions of government subsidies. Also, it would provide some degree of job creation without massive capital outlays. A meeting with the Urban Municipalities Association of Canada should be held at the earliest opportunity. If an incentive structure can be set up with small grants being made to the communities to cause them to move in this direction, this will provide a useful direction in the whole area of housing for lower-income people in this country.
Let me get back to the selective economic stimulus of new housing construction. Building a very modest house requires one man-year of direct house construction labour. A mediumsized house will provide two man-years of skilled labour employment and a more spacious dwelling, three to four man-years.
How is the construction of housing for middle and high-income earners to be stimulated so that jobs can be generated today without a massive infusion of government capital? One possible course of action is to provide selective incentives through the tax system, in other words, tax perks that produce new wealth and create jobs. I realize the government has removed most of the tax perks which tend to provide new wealth or jobs.
If the government had the political courage, it could give serious consideration to providing mortgage interest rate cost deductibility above a base figure of 10 per cent or even 8 per cent on new houses built and marketed only in the next two to five years. This would act as an incentive for middle and higher-income people to build more homes and provide job creation.
One could argue this would be subsidies for the rich or middle-income earners. However, if one considers that the intent of the policy would be job creation without inflation and without government borrowings, it might be considered seriously. Why not? What can government lose? Its revenues would increase rather than decrease. Such incentives would automatically disappear when interest rates again drop to reasonable levels. Therefore, the incentives would be of short duration.
With regard to selective stimulation, why can the government not permit borrowing interest costs on the purchase of Canadian-made cars, those with a certain percentage of Canadian content, as income tax deductible items for the next one or two years? Ontario stimulated car sales substantially
February 17, 1982

with a similar program. The federal government would surely end up in the black rather than in the red with such a short-term policy.
Many other examples of selective stimulation for meeting the two conditions I laid down earlier are possible. I hope that a task force can be put together at the earliest opportunity to come forth with a whole series of programs by government for selectively stimulating the Canadian economy and creating jobs without necessarily increasing inflation.
I now want to dwell very briefly on the megaprojects, particularly the Alsands plant north of Fort McMurray and the Cold Lake heavy oil plant. Let me say that megaprojects are rapidly evolving a new form of enterprise. These massive projects require enormous capital and cross literally every level of enterprise; social, economic public and private. They have assumed the characteristics more closely resembling massive utility projects rather than high-risk capital enterprise projects. They are evolving as government and private sector partnerships rather than pure private enterprise partnerships. Government involvement is almost mandatory to reduce political risk on such massive projects and guarantees not only an energy source, but rapid recovery of the massive capital outlay.
1 want to indicate that when we first dealt with Syncrude, the extent of capital involvement was nowhere near the level required in an oil sands plant today. We talked about somewhat under a billion dollars. These costs are now reflected in the order of $12 billion to $15 billion. The capital requirements are massive. Therefore, the risks must be minimized in every possible way.
The basic requirement for bringing into reality a project such as the heavy oil plant in Cold Lake or the Alsands plant is government involvement in a minority equity position and massive involvement in building the community infrastructure and transportation facilities. The private sector likes to see the government involved in a minority equity position so that it can reduce its risk and guarantee success of the subject in the longer term.
The second requirement is a guaranteed rate of return on invested capital following normal utilities, in a general way. This would assure product price structures on the short and long term.
The third requirement is rapid capital investment recovery for redeployment of such capital. The fourth requirement is the total remission of all federal government taxes and provincial government royalties during the early life of the projects so as to reduce risks and assure capital recovery and recycling over the shortest possible time-frame. Simply, the government must delay its tax revenues and royalties on plants of this type to the period after investment capital is recovered in order to provide both the spark and inertia to make such plants a reality.
In my opinion, the Alsands project is dying rapidly, and it will take a miracle to revive it. The priorities on the Cold Lake heavy oil project should have been and must be reviewed.
Taxation
Alsands required a massive new infrastructure and transportation system, most of which is now in place in the Cold Lake facility. The Alsands plant is the third such plant, and the technology is fully commercialized so that new plants can await a more favourable interest rate climate. The Cold Lake plant is the first of its kind. It involves the commercialization of a new technology related to a heavy oil reserve in the order of 40 billion to 50 billion barrels of oil. The environmental consequences are minimal when compared to the Alsands plant. Furthermore, the ability to raise vast capital requirements is enhanced by the very nature of the possible government-industry partnership at Cold Lake.
I remember the early negotiations on the Great Canadian Oilsands plant. I also remember the early discussions and the manner in which Syncrude had to be saved. These projects involved relatively mild capital requirements when compared to both the Cold Lake plant and the Alsands plant. No knowledgeable or experienced industry partnership would invest $13 billion in one area unless it was guaranteed a rate of return on investment and guaranteed a price for its product. It must recover that capital over the shortest possible time-frame. Surely governments can make all their money after the first five or ten years of operation when, in fact, most of the invested capital is recovered. Government should regard these projects as effectively being utility plants providing energy at a reasonable rate of return on investment.
I wrote a letter to the Premier of Alberta and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the fall of 1980 to indicate that the Cold Lake plant was the First of its kind and we were involved in the commercialization of a technology which had not been commercially proven anywhere in the world. The reserves associated with that technology, 50 billion barrels of heavy oil in place, were enough to serve Canada for many years to come. The Cold Lake heavy oil plant must be revived at the earliest opportunity and this can only be done by providing an incentive climate which would minimize the economic risk. 1 believe that the two governments must get together as soon as possible and develop that climate and provide for the Cold Lake project a total federal crude oil tax and provincial royalty remission until the investment capital is fully recovered. A second necessary requirement is an established product price regime for at least the first ten years of the production cycle, followed by a tracking of world price thereafter. As I have said earlier, inflation and high interest rates have required a somewhat different format from that which made Syncrude a reality. Surely this new format can be negotiated and evolved in Canada's interest.
The failure or indefinite postponement of the Cold Lake heavy oil project is a national disgrace. In my estimation, it is tantamount to a form of national treason. What other nation can look to a reserve of 50 billion barrels of heavy oil? What other nation can look to a developed process which has had a pilot plant running for several years? What other nation can look to having a company which is developing a regime to build a plant in the order of $12 billion to $15 billion to

generate 140,000 barrels of oil per day? Throughout our discussions, we have allowed this to fail.
Perhaps I have strayed somewhat from the pertinent aspects of Bill C-93, but the reason I rose to speak today was to indicate that the government should be seriously thinking of entering into a phase of selective economic stimulus. I agree that inflation is our primary problem and it must be reduced at the earliest opportunity. Economic stimulation can be achieved without increasing the government debt or increasing inflation, with the primary concern being job creation. Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for giving me this opportunity to speak briefly on this matter.

It is interesting to note in passing that a one-time prominent member of the Liberal government, C. D. Howe, created a national storm by remarking, in response to an accusation of monetary inaccuracy, "What's a million?". That is what he said at that time. If he were alive today, he would have to say, "What's a billion?" to even draw the slightest attention to monetary maleficence. This is the extent to which successive Liberal governments have inoculated the Canadian public against the disease of financial mismanagement. Canadians have come to expect government financial mismanagement to the extent that million dollar errors no longer shock the public. The $500 million loss at Mirabel, the $600 million debt write-off for the St. Lawrence Seaway, the $450 million to $550 million annual losses in the post office are hardly even newsworthy. What Canada needs is a billion dollar fiasco to attract sufficient public attention. The government is working hard to achieve this objective of a billion dollar fiasco which will draw attention to the financial plight of Canada.
Apart from changes in excise and sales tax of a relatively technical nature, the other major thrust of Bill C-93 is the implementation of a price and tax regime which will now be imposed on energy supplies, particularly oil and natural gas. I do not intend to review the mechanics of these tax measures, but 1 will consider the energy problem in Canada since it has such a gigantic impact on our financial position and our economic future.
Let me now consider the budget, recognizing that Bill C-93 is part of that ongoing process. What I want to do first is try to reduce the motivation for the 1981 budget to understandable and general terms. In order to do that it is almost necessary to review the 1980 budget which was introduced in the House of Commons on October 28, 1980. In that budget, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), in explaining the financial plan of the government for that year, commented on the tax structure and said:
-I turn now to questions of taxation. I have a special responsibility to ensure that our tax system is fair and that it contributes to the achievement of our economic and social objectives. On the whole, our tax system is one of the best in the world. Canada's individual and corporate taxes were lower than in many other industrialized countries, including the United States.
In October of 1980 the Minister of Finance was pleased to speak in glowing terms of Canada's tax system but, strangely enough, just a year and a month later, on November 12, 1981, when he introduced the 1981 version of his budgetary process, he said in his budget speech:
Many Canadians find our tax system unfair, and I agree with them. They realize that taxes are necessary to pay for important government services, but they feel that rates of tax are too high. They sense that others, the well-advised or the wealthy, very often pay less than their fair share.
What we have in two successive budget speeches is the Minister of Finance contradicting his view of Canada's tax system. On the one hand, in 1980, he said it was one of the best tax systems in the world, and then a year later he said it was unfair and that people had said it was unfair. The Minister of Finance has never stated, in the House or in any other place of which I am aware, who said the tax system was unfair or what was the claim of unfairness in the tax system the Minister of Finance was asked to remedy. If we knew what the claim of unfairness was with respect to the tax system- and I hasten to add that there certainly are measures which are unfair-and if we knew exactly who made the claim of unfairness and what their claim involved, then we could deal with that, but we were not allowed that opportunity. The Minister of Finance simply announced in 1980 that we had a good tax system and in 1981 that we had a tax system which was unfair. This would lead one to believe that the Minister of Finance was simply using the tax system to bring about changes which he had in mind to make; that is to say, he was not responding to any initiative from the public. He was not responding to any thrust from the business world, any thrust from the world of education, any thrust from the world of finance or any thrust from any other of the segments which make up our Canadian society. He was simply engaged in an internal operation of introducing some tax measures, the real
February 17, 1982

result of which was to gain more revenue for the federal Treasury.
What we are faced with in the budget is simply an exercise whereby, under the guise of reform of the tax system, the Minister of Finance is introducing measures which will bring more dollars into the federal treasury.
1 ought to answer the question: why does the federal government need more dollars in its Treasury? The answer is very simple. Years of overspending and financial mismanagement have led to a situation in which drastic action must be taken, but unfortunately, the only resource left to tax in Canada is the hard-working people of Canada who engage in enterprise and who work for wages for a living. They are the only resource from which money can be drawn, and that is what the government is doing, but it is doing it under the guise of reforming the tax system.
There are other methods of reforming a tax system, and I ought to deal with the fact that in the past these methods have been reviewed at great length. Over a decade ago the Carter commission examined in great detail the tax system in Canada and came up with very serious recommendations which would perhaps have led to a fairer tax system for all Canadians. But at that time there were members of the government and members of the Liberal Party who rose up and said that those reforms would not come about, that the recommendations of the Carter commission would not be implemented in Canada and that they wanted the tax system we now have in place. That consultative process, which went on over a long period of time and dealt with the Canadian tax system in detail, was simply chucked out the window because of Members of Parliament like Senator Olson, who now resides in the other place and not in the House of Commons. Perhaps it is for that reason he rejected out of hand tax reforms and opted for the system the Minister of Finance now tells us has to be changed in the way he has changed it.
There was another thrust in the 1981 budget which would have gained the support of most people in Canada, and that was the government's promise to reduce the deficit. In his budget speech the Minister of Finance said he would reduce the deficit of the Government of Canada over a period of two or three years by $4 billion to $6 billion. I think he said approximately $5 billion by 1984.
How are the government and the Minister of Finance proposing to reduce that deficit? Their proposal is simply to deprive the provinces of funds in the form of transfer payments, equalization payments and payments made under established programs funding. What the government really proposes in the 1981 budget, in the name of reducing the deficit, is to transfer the deficit to the provinces of Canada. More important, the provinces of Canada to which this deficit will be transferred will be the provinces which can least afford to carry that deficit. They are the provinces which are now required, because of their lack of financial capacity, to seek assistance from the federal government. I am talking primarily about the Atlantic provinces of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, but the province of
Taxation
Quebec also benefits from these programs, as do the western provinces and the province of Ontario with respect to specific programs. These provinces can ill afford to bear the federal deficit. These provinces are already burdened. Nova Scotia has a deficit of about a quarter of a billion dollars which, in terms of population, is very substantial. Hon. members may not be aware that the province of Prince Edward Island, for example, spends more money per capita on providing services within that province than any other province of Canada, approximately $3,000 a year per citizen. The other maritime provinces pay similar amounts. That is because those provinces do not have economic advantages. This is the region that sutfers from economic disparity. Because of this, the strain on government is greater. The people need more services and more assistance in terms of social welfare payments, education and all the services government has to provide, particularly in areas where the population cannot provide for itself to the extent it can in other parts of Canada.
The reduction of the deficit is not really a reduction which will benefit the financial situation across Canada or balance the books, so to speak, of government. It will simply transfer that debt to another level of government, a level of government which can least afford to carry the debt, and it will not be able to carry that kind of debt without raising taxes or without reducing services.
There are two main thrusts to the budget-reduction of the deficit and the reform of the tax system. The Economic Council of Canada has confirmed that the claim of reducing the federal deficit is false, that it is simply a matter of refinancing some of the government's assistance to the provinces and, as a result, the deficit will be carried by the provinces.
We know from people who have complained to us directly and in the press that the government's claim of tax reform is false, and that the claim that equity and fairness will be brought into the tax system is also false.
I can explode that myth with some facts and figures, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of Finance told us in this House that under the new tax measures approximately 12 million taxpayers will pay less tax, that 3.5 million will pay the same amount of taxes and that only 800,000 will pay more. Those statistics have been challenged again and again, not just by members of this House but by the Canadian Labour Congress and by tax experts like Mr. Arthur Drache who, in an article, indicated that at least two million Canadians would be paying more tax in the 1982 taxation year.
The almost seven million Canadians who participate in health and dental care programs and receive financial assistance with respect to those programs from their employers will be taxed on the financial contribution made by or allocated to the employer. So as many as seven million Canadians and certainly at least four million Canadians will be facing increased taxes because of that measure.

February 17, 1982

Another consideration is the provision with respect to the taxation of insurance benefits as they accrue. There are 13 million policyholders across Canada, 40 per cent of whom earn under $25,000 per year and 60 per cent of the policies are for less than $50,000 per year. Pensioners will also have to pay increased taxes because they will lose the $1,000 pension deduction if they are contributing to an RRSP. Approximately 2.3 million senior citizens in Canada receive old age assistance and almost two million receive the guaranteed income supplement. About 2.5 million Canadians over age 65 may be adversely affected by these tax measures. When we complain about the measures contained in the budget, we are not talking about the business community or the high priced executive; we are talking about 2.5 million senior citizens and the seven million Canadians who receive assistance through health and dental plans. In other words, we are talking about the ordinary people that this budget attacks.
These people may not be too aware now of the price they will have to pay but they will know all about it next year when they file their income tax returns and find that they must pay tax on their health and dental plans, and that they cannot deduct the interest on payments made to an RRSP for which they borrowed funds. A year from now pensioners will know that they will not be able to use the $1,000 deduction.
It is our job, in this House, to get the word out to the Canadian people so that they may respond to these measures. That is exactly what we have done, Mr. Speaker. This party had a special committee on the budget and the economy which travelled across Canada. It was a forum at which interested persons could register their complaints and ask questions about the budget and its measures. If Canadians want to protect themselves against these unfair measures they have to act now. We know that they are acting now because they are writing to Members of Parliament on this side and on the government side. I do not think any member on the government side could say that he or she is not receiving complaints from constituents-from pensioners, the ordinary workers and construction workers who will be taxed on housing benefits.
The government is backing off, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey) has backed off the measure to tax travel passes issued to transport workers. The budget provided that the passes issued to the 45,000 transport workers of Air Canada and CN would be taxed on their market value. There was such an outcry that the government knew 45,000 votes would be lost, so the minister issued a paper stating that was not what was intended at all, that the passes were not to be taxed at market value but only on a certain percentage. The gobbledygook is all written out in the statement issued by the minister, Mr. Speaker. There are no regulations to back this up but I suppose they will be issued as soon as the minister figures how they can work things out without contradicting the budget proposal.
If the 1.2 million of the 2.5 million pensioners in Canada who face the loss of the $1,000 pension deduction protest, the government will back off that provision as well. I do not know how the transport workers got the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Finance to issue that paper. Perhaps the pensioners could get in touch with them and find out what is going on.
It appears that the government is willing to back off because it wants to save its political hide. It has to save it or it will lose the next election. This is not like their promise on the energy tax where they told the people to vote for them and then there would be no increase in the price of gasoline. They told people not to worry about the 18 cents.

1 should like to change the record. The province of Prince Edward Island pays 50 per cent of its revenue on education and health; the province of Nova Scotia pays 42 per cent; the province of Newfoundland, for the information of the minister, pays 45.6 per cent out of total government expenditures.
Now I should like to deal with the point raised by the Minister of National Revenue. I cannot explain it because it is simply the numbers game. The Government of Canada says, "Here are the numbers"; the provinces say, "Here are the numbers". But what counts is the dollars which flow through to the institutions providing educational services or to the hospitals and persons providing health, hospital and medical services. They are the ones who say that the dollars are not coming through.
Whether one blames the provinces or the federal government, it is just a numbers game. My answer to the minister is that it is a numbers game. But I should like to say something to the president of Memorial University in Newfoundland. In 1982 he will not receive as many dollars as he thinks he should; in 1983 it will be less; and in 1984 it will be even less than 1983. This will be the result of changes in federal government policy. He can blame it on the province of New-

foundland as well. It is up to him. He can work out the numbers, but he will receive fewer dollars.
I am very glad the Minister of National Revenue focused attention on this matter. The president of Memorial University will be faced with some choices-he will have to cut services in the university, raise tuition fees, or find other methods of financing through alumni contributions or funds from the private sector. Those will be his choices. I believe he will have to employ all of them. He will have to cut services at Memorial University, raise student tuition fees, and look for funding from the private sector. He will not be in the same position he would have been in if the federal government had really and truly continued its contributions at the rates provided in the past and had not become involved in cutbacks.
Not just universities, but hospitals and a wide variety of government services will have to cut back or raise taxes. There is no avoiding it. When the dollars flow through, they will not be in the amount they have been traditionally as a result of government policy to reduce its deficit and pass it on to the provinces. It is as simple as the man in advertising who says, "You can pay me now or you can pay me later." I am saying that it will happen. I will have to wait a year or two, but the minister will be forced to admit in the House, that it has happened. The money will not be there. Hospital, medical and educational services will be cut back, and taxes will be raised. I am referring to provinces which cannot carry the deficit.
I do not know about the province of Alberta; it is very ably represented in the House and those members will speak to that problem. But what about the province of Quebec? The Premier of Quebec, Rene Levesque, has stood up time and time again and said that it will happen. It will happen, and when it happens hon. members from that province who did not speak out as 1 am speaking out now will be faced with the problem and fixed with the responsibility. I suspect that is why ten of them signed the letter which outlined the situation in point form. They know it will happen. They know services will be cut in health, education and other social fields. They know taxes will be raised and that educational institutions will be required to seek private funding.
I think I have said enough about the concerns of the provinces and the transfer of deficits as a result of the budget. Now I want to deal with some tax measures which affect individual Canadians. I have already referred to some of them, but first I would like to indicate how I know about this. I was a member of the special committee on the budget and the economy. I was appointed by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). It was with great foresight and interest in individual Canadians that he set up this committee, so ably chaired by the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson). We travelled around the country and talked with people. Members of the committee reached out and said, "What do you think of the budget? Here it is, let us discuss it." We wanted to hear what the people thought and travelled to many places across Canada, and we heard from the people of Canada. It was a new exercise, but it was a very important one. It allowed us to be in contact with the people.
