The Minister of National Revenue is not fooling anyone in the House. He has been in touch with people, he knows that they are complaining, and he wants to respond to their concerns. The important point is that we put the concerns on record. People know what is happening, and they knew it before the budget was finalized. They are making their complaints now, and they are timely. The government is starting to withdraw. On December 18 the minister stood in the House and withdrew some provisions and modified others. The Minister of National Revenue, left to his own devices, attempted to achieve some justice within his regulatory power and within the regulatory power of his department. I think he will do more.
I want to detail some particular tax measures respecting pension income deductions which are of great concern. First and foremost, I am interested in senior citizens; I hope to be one some day. Under the law as 1 understand it, a person in receipt of pension income can deduct $1,000 from his or her total income, which includes pension income. It will be taken away if the person contributes to a registered retirement savings plan. If an executive of a large corporation, such as Imperial Oil or some goliath, retires early, receives pension benefits, a new yacht and everything else, and because of his great wealth continues to contribute to an RRSP, I would not even stand in the House to defend him. Such persons will not be affected. But thousands of retired Armed Forces personnel across the country who retired early because of the pension system in the Armed Forces will be affected. In order to maintain themselves they are forced to seek other employment. There are thousands of public servants in the same position who retired early with small pensions, continued to work, and naturally contributed to registered retirement savings plans. The government has come along and is taxing those persons by taking away their $1,000 deduction simply because some corporate executive will receive the same benefit.
We know that you do not have to hit every pensioner, whether over 65 or not, who continues to work. Why are people doing this? It is being done because people receive a smaller pension at an earlier age, an age when they are still able to work. They know down the line when they reach their senior years that they will not be able to work and they are trying to provide sufficient income for those years. Surely those are not the people who ought to be attacked by the Government of Canada, the Parliament of Canada. As a parliamentarian, I do not want to be any part of that attack.
Now we come to the registered retirement savings plans. Again the government is coming in with a gun to kill that. Certainly there has been a little abuse of registered retirement savings plans. People who do not need to provide for retirement are involved with them, but the people who borrow money to contribute to a registered retirement savings plan are in the early stages of their activity-for instance, young engineers who hope later on, if they get a job and continue to be employed, they will have enough money to continue to contribute to the plan and pay off the debt. They are the ones who are
taking advantage of the interest borrowing advantage, not the corporate executive or the millionaire. They do not need to borrow money to contribute to a registered retirement savings plan. That is a lot of nonsense, Mr. Speaker. The ordinary people are the ones who are borrowing for an RRSP. We wish the government would come to its sense about that.
Then we have life insurance. About 14 million people across Canada have life insurance. Are you telling me, Mr. speaker, that the Minister of Finance really believes that these people are trying to gyp the tax man? Of course not; these people are trying to provide for their families. That is the Canadian tradition. If I had an unfortunate accident, which the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans) might like to see happen, and I did not have the ability to earn income for my family, 1 would want some life insurance to take its place. That is perfectly reasonable. I am not trying to avoid taxes, yet the government wants to tax that accrual. Really, who is the government trying to kid? Canadians are not trying to cheat anyone. Canadians are trying to provide for their families and there is no reason for this type of thing to be taxed.
Next there is the health and dental plans. There are four million Canadians covered by health and dental plans. In the private sector alone there are another million who are covered by the employer-employee arrangement that has been worked out through collective bargaining. There are another 500,000 involved with union health plans in the building trades. There are probably another two million people involved with Blue Cross and other non-profit institutions that provide health and dental care. Maybe as many as seven million Canadians and probably 11 million are covered, and the government steps in and says "This is not available to all Canadians; it is a tax dodge. You are trying to give a benefit instead of dollars; therefore, we will tax you." But that is not true. Those plans are there to help people and to see that they get adequate medical care, particularly dental care. If they do not have such plans, they will not get the care. If people have to pay tax, the plans will be endangered because people will say "Give me the money and I will pay for it myself." Then the plans will collapse. That is what the government is doing. The government has to back off from doing this.
Now I shall talk about capital cost allowance. That is in the business field. In my travels I learned that as a result of the change in the capital cost allowance, the first year allowance will be reduced to 50 per cent or one half. For example, this will mean that car rental companies who are used to taking the larger allowance, the faster write-off in the first year will be forced to hold on to a car for another year. They usually hold them for two years; now it will be three years. They purchase
45,000	to 60,000 cars in Canada each year. It will mean a reduction of one third in car purchases if they cannot take up this write-off. What will that do to the automobile industry? It will mean a loss of 15,000 or 20,000 sales. Yet the Government of Canada is contributing to the automobile industry by financing it and trying to keep it afloat. The government is contributing public funds to the automobile industry, and the
February 17, 1982

government is taking away 15,000 to 20,000 sales of cars a year by a tax measure. Who is going forward and backward on that? How ridiculous can you get? We will not let the government get away with that.
Now to the positive side. Let me talk about child care. The government knows that Canadians who have to maintain a child in separate accommodation outside a home have to pay more for that service than the tax system allows, but the government does not do anything about that. 1 could go on and talk about that but in my last two minutes I want to talk about unemployment.
We can talk about the economy, but the big thing is employment. We have to keep Canadians employed. We have a labour force of over 11 million people, but 1.2 million people are out of work. That is not only an economic problem but a social problem. I read an article by a psychiatrist, Dr. Thomson, who comes from my constituency. He pointed out this problem very graphically. We have to solve these problems on a positive note.
We can beat this economic situation in Canada. All we have to do is get the energy projects going, the offshore projects and the Alberta tar sands. We should take advantage of our strengths and build on them. Our object, however, is to provide jobs for people. That is what people want. If people can get work they will pay their bills. Canadians still have incentive. They still want to work and contribute, but unfortunately it is the Government of Canada that is standing in their way.
Strangely enough, the government is not getting the projects going. The energy projects are stalled. They will take place; the tar sands will be developed some time, but they might as well be developed now. The offshore resources have to be explored. That exploration might as well start now. We are not saving anything. We have the manufacturing components. Let us not let things die because we have economic reversal. We have to create economic activity. We have to create jobs. We have to provide jobs for Canadians. This is no time for economic purism. This is no time for people to say "We have a long-range plan to reduce inflation; that will cause this and this will cause that." How do we know? Because some economist in a tax book says so? We are dealing with people. Canadians are the ones who determine what they want. Canadians are the ones who determine what the government must do. What Canadians want is economic activity; they want job creation. This government ought to give it to them. It is the right thing to do and it will have the best result.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-93 asks for a borrowing authority of some $6.6 billion this year. In the first year I was a Member of Parliament, the government asked for borrowing auhority of some $14 billion. In my second year as a Member of Parliament, that borrowing authority was reduced to some $12 billion. I see this year it is now $6.6 billion. It appears that the government is likely making some progress in reducing its deficit. But the reason the amount has been reduced so dramatically has to do with the responsibility for the debt that has been incurred by the federal government in its policies. It
Taxation
has transferred the responsibility for payment of that debt to the provinces and municipal governments. For instance, the community services contribution program; I think of the transfer of the increased costs of the RCMP and policing services. Many municipalities and provincial governments saw this as a dire hardship.
Another area on which I will dwell at some length is the Crow rate and the government's intention to abolish this statutory and historic rate. The Crowsnest Pass agreement was a continuation of national policy when it was first started. The national policy of which I speak is the banding together of the country from the Pacific to the Atlantic by a ribbon of steel, so to speak, the railway that should have been in place. The major aspect was a publicly subsidized, privately owned transcontinental rail network. In 1897 the only rail line into the mineral rich Kootenay region of B.C. was a branch line of the American Great Northern Railway which had reached Nelson in 1895. This was perceived as a threat to Canadian sovereignty and the region provided Canadian Pacific with sufficient leverage to extract some $3.4 million and 3.7 million acres of land from the federal and British Columbia governments to finance the construction of a 300-mile line from Lethbridge, Alberta, through the Crowsnest Pass to Nelson.
During the same period of time political pressure from the west had brought the federal government to the realization that exorbitant freight rates arising from the monopoly power of the rail companies were working against another goal of national policy, that being the rapid settlement and agricultural development on the prairies which was essential. This realization was reflected in the other half of the Crowsnest Pass agreement whereby Canadian Pacific agreed to reduce certain of its rates, including grain and flour, on commodities moving from the west to the Lakehead, and they were to remain there indefinitely.
During the time from 1903 until about 1918, Mr. Speaker, during which time the War Measures Act was invoked because of World War I, the rates fluctuated drastically but the producers did not really complain a great deal because of the overriding national interest in preserving our freedom during time of war. However, in 1922 the rates were restored under pressure from the west, with opposition by the railway interests, because they had really fluctuated quite wildly during that period of time.
Then in 1925 the rates were fixed by statute and extended to cover shipments to the Lakehead on any line in the west, including those built after 1897. The rates were extended in 1927 to the shipment of grain and flour to west coast ports for export, and to the port of Churchill in 1931. In 1961 raw oilseeds were added to the Crow rate structure which now applied to western rapeseed meal going to Thunder Bay but not Vancouver. Rapeseed oils move at regular rates but western shippers received a federal freight subsidy on shipments to western markets.

The Crow rate has, since its inception, been regarded in the west as a sort of balance, Mr. Speaker, to the benefits that central Canada has always derived at the expense of the rest of the country from the tariff wall protecting its industry. One question which often comes to mind for many of my constituents, Mr. Speaker, is: does the Crow rate really affect the quality of service in grain movement by rail in western Canada? The statutory freight rates have given prairie grain farmers effective protection from a railway monopoly over rate setting. They provide no such protection when it comes to the level of service the railways provide, nor does the Railway Act. In fact, the quality of service has been poor for a very long time. Grain cars have generally been poorly maintained. I stand to be corrected, but I believe the last time CN and CP actually purchased cars for the movement of grain was back in the early 1950s, and they have certainly deteriorated since that time. They are obsolete and in short supply. The track and roadbeds have been allowed to deteriorate, and as a result sales opportunities have been lost. The cars produced lately have been at the expense of either the federal or provincial governments, or the producers themselves.
At the moment the railways cover their grain transportation costs from three different sources of income: the producer, who pays the statutory freight rate; the federal government, which pays the railways a subsidy of about $100 million a year for continued service on uneconomical branch lines; and the balance comes from other sectors, possibly from the transportation of other commodities.
The federal government has in recent years assumed some costs directly, such as the provision of hopper cars, as I mentioned, and also the rehabilitation of branch lines throughout many points in Canada. Nevertheless, the railways still seem to lose some money on carrying grain. Just how much is uncertain, but estimates range from $60 million to $400 million a year. And the quality of service is still inadequate. They cannot say they are putting this money into upgrading the line or the service they are providing.
Furthermore, planned increases in production of grain will require the elimination of a number of bottlenecks in the transportation system, Mr. Speaker, but the railways argue that unless the Crow goes they will not be able to finance these investments. Although the railways may lose some money on the actual movement of grain, if you look at the profit figures of the railway companies you will see that in 1970 CN had a net loss of some $30 million. But if you move up to 1980, one decade later, they have a profit of $193 million. CP Rail had a profit in 1970 of $24 million. A decade later they have a profit of $122 million.
However, the point that particularly bothers some people about CP's profit is that it does not all go into the rail service they are supposedly providing to the Canadian public and producer. It goes into such things as Canadian Pacific Limited, where they have chosen to invest much of the money they should have been investing in the actual railway system which should be part of our economic and industrial strategy. In 1980, Mr. Speaker, Canadian Pacific Limited had a profit of
some $583 million. So I find it hard to believe that the railways are hard pressed and losing money.
The situation has led many western grain growers and farm organizations to seek some other method of ensuring that more money goes into improving the railways' performance in moving grain, Mr. Speaker. The following positions have been developed by different organizations in western Canada. For example, the National Farmers Union says that the Crow rate is not negotiable, a position I agree with. It must remain as part of an over-all transportation policy which recognizes the needs of rural communities, and should be extended to other crops and processed products as well. The railways should be compelled to provide adequate service. The railway companies' over-all profits, including their non-rail enterprises, are very high and I have given a few examples. If they refuse to cover the grain transportation shortfalls through internal corporate transfers, then they should be integrated and operated as a public utility to serve the national interest.

They are supported in this by several of the livestock producer organizations, and by the Conservative government of Alberta. This is a position which this party certainly disagrees with. We do not think the Crow rate should be negotiable and opened up on the table to be chopped away at, further reducing what has sometimes been a very small profit margin for the farmers.

Another question which arises quite often is whether the Crow is a barrier to economic development in the west. The western cattle feeders, in particular, see the Crow rate as contributing to the already high cost of feed grains on the prairies which, in turn, puts the prairie livestock industry at a disadvantage relative to its eastern counterparts. 1 disagree with that. 1 do not think it stops economic development in the west. However, the reasoning is that the price at which grain growers are willing to sell feed grains on the prairies is closely related to what is called the farm gate price of export grains-for example, the world price of grain in export positions in Vancouver and Thunder Bay, minus the freight charges, actually paid by the grower to get it to the port.
If the grower had to pay the higher rates on the movement of export grain, the effective farm gate price would automatically fall, presumably to an amount equal to the difference between the Crow and the new higher rates. The logical result would be that there would be cheaper feed for prairie cattle and hog producers, and it would encourage oilseed crushing and flour mills in the west. The cheaper food would mean higher incomes for cattlemen, I suppose, but the theory might not work through into the practicality of the situation. There is no guarantee that these increases in cattle prices, which I do not think are there, would offset the disastrous economic effect on the farmers in western Canada.
I think there is an alternative proposal which should be considered as opposed to the position of the federal government at the present time. The government is holding closed sessions across Canada which is a real violation of the democracy of this country in that there should be open and public input into the discussions which are centring around the one-man commission which has been set up by the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). An alternative proposal which would get around this problem while retaining the Crow rate included in the recommendation of the Hall commission report and the Grain Handling Transportation Commission of 1977 that subsidized freight rates be applied on the transportation by rail of meat, processed grain and oilseed products from the west to eastern markets. This position is supported by the National Farmers Union and the New Democratic Party. 1 think this is a good position, it would do much more toward strengthening the ties across Canada and would do a much greater job of helping the producers of western Canada increase their profitability picture somewhat.
In this party we are very fearful that, once the statutory rates are tampered with, there will be talk about variable rates. The current statutory rates are related to distance. It costs the grower half a cent to ship a ton of wheat one mile by rail, no matter to which elevator on the line the wheat is delivered. For the railways, it cost more to handle grain through many low volume elevators on low volume branch lines. In addition to wanting more money for every bushel of grain they carry, the railways would like to have a means of persuading the farmers to truck their grain to a relatively smaller number of high volume, inland terminals on main lines. Variable rates, in

other words, would do just that, and we do not want variable rates to come in.
The only way the railways could get the farmers to pay this higher cost of trucking their grain to the inland terminals rather than delivering to the nearest local elevator would be to charge a higher rate per ton mile for serving the local elevator. In effect, variable rates would provide the railways with a device for reorganizing the prairie grain handling system so as to minimize their operating costs without the nuisance of public branch line abandonment hearings. However, efficiency for the railways would be achieved at considerable cost to the other systems that we have in place on the prairies. If there were no grain handling system providing the focal point for the producers, the farming community and the ranching community around small prairie towns, many of those small towns would have a hard time existing. The larger centres would, in fact, grow and flourish, and that is not a way of life that we relish in most of the provinces in western Canada.
The existing prairie branch line network and the country elevator system could quite possibly even disappear. The farmers would be burdened with higher and rapidly increasing trucking costs for hauling longer distances, and elevator companies would likely be stuck with hundreds of elevators abandoned by the producers. Many of the rural communities would lose their principal reason for existence, and the provincial governments would have to absorb an increase in road maintenance costs resulting from much heavier traffic.
Looking back in time, one wonders why the railway companies accepted this Crow rate at the time. 1 think it was well put in the book "Canadian Transportation Economics" written by A.W. Currie in 1967. In discussing the reason Canadian Pacific accepted the deal in 1897, Mr. Currie stated:
Sir William Van Horne, then general manager of the Canadian Pacific, has been credited with enormous vision because he saw that low rates would induce new settlement, increase the volume and profitability of the railway's traffic, and enormously enhance the value of the company's extensive holdings of land.
I think that latter comment certainly describes the high priority of Canadian Pacific, because it has certainly utilized those land holdings to its best advantage and not to the advantage of a railway system within this country of ours.
One quite often wonders whether the transportation system would get better if variable rates were removed. If we paid more to the rail companies, would they move our product in a better manner?

The revenue problem caused by the Crow rate is recognized to some extent. Grain accounts for about 13 per cent of the loaded freight car miles and therefore for about 13 per cent of the workload and the expense of Canadian railways. However, the taxpayers have been meeting a good portion of that gap through such programs as branch line subsidies, rail rehabilitation, and absorbing interest on the cost of hopper cars.

The share of the hauling of the grain is expected to drop even more during the 1980s. By the year 1990, the volume of grain hauled on the Canadian rail network is expected to be only between 12 per cent and 14 per cent of their total volume.
The federal government and the railways claim that the Crow rate provides the western grain farmers with a unique advantage, but I do not think it does. In 1980, federal government transport subsidies across Canada totalled some $2.4 billion. Of that total, only $284 million related to the prairie grain movement. In short, transportation subsidies have always been used as an instrument to achieve national goals and objectives within this country. If the Crow rate is eliminated, livestock producers will be in a worse competitive position in western Canada. Do the railways or the federal government seriously suggest that the livestock industry in western Canada will expand at a time when market prices are 30 cents to 40 cents per pound below the cost of production? 1 do not believe that livestock producers in western Canada will gain any advantage by removing the Crow rate. In fact, with the attitude of this government, I do not know what advantage any Canadian will have.
Let us consider the federal plan. At one time the federal policy was to guarantee statutory protection for the producer because of the monopolistic concept of the railway system. The federal government has now decided to reverse this fundamental principle in the belief that the railways need protection from the farmers.
Second, the plan of the federal government is to eliminate a fixed rate for producers. Just as important as the level of the Crow rate is the fact that it is a rate for the producers which has been guaranteed by statute. It is not a rate which any railway, quasi-judicial body or any order in council can wipe out at will. It is a rate upon which Canadian producers could depend as a fixed figure in helping them plan their future during uncertain times.
As I mentioned earlier, the federal plan provides no protection for the principle of equal rates for equal distance. If this principle is removed it will have disastrous consequences for those rural communities to which the Crow rate applies.
The federal government has indicated that it recognizes the need for railway modernization in western Canada. Moderni-

zation is not only needed on the prairies but in British Columbia and other parts of Canada. Instead of giving handouts to the railways from the Canadian taxpayer or at the expense of prairie farmers, our party proposes that the anticipated $2.1 billion in additional capital be provided by the federal government and participating provincial governments jointly in return for equity. In other words, we will build the rail system but we would want some equity in that system as well.
I would like to quote for the record what the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) had to say recently. He said:
If farmers operated under the business principles of the railways, they would stop growing food and invest in shopping centres or oil wells. Were it not for a dedicated farm population taking low-sometimes no-return on their labour and investment, Canada would go hungry.
This could very well be our problem in the future. The government will have to borrow more than $6.6 billion if it continues to erode its economic policies and erode our transpo-ration system which is such an important part of Canada's industrial strategy. We cannot put these debts on the backs of the other governments which have already been given more debts than they should be asked to absorb. If a crisis situation arises in our agricultural industry due to the government's attitude and its policies, we will be borrowing much more than $6.6 billion.
The New Democratic Party believes that 100 per cent improved rail capacity would support even greater borrowing authority to ensure that we had the best rail system in the world to serve all producers. We cannot support a change in the rate unless the government improves the railway system, and not only at the farmers' expense because they are an important part of the whole Canadian economy. The government reaps billions of dollars from the agricultural industry which it uses to reduce part of Canada's trade deficits to other countries. This money not only comes from the producers in the western provinces but from Quebec and rural communities in Ontario, which is a fact that should be emphasized.
There is a contradiction in all this. On the one hand, the government proudly proclaims that Canada's exports will increase substantially to 30 million metric tons by 1985-86. Under the agri-food strategy, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) claims that grain production for the prairies will increase by 77 per cent to 100 per cent in the next 25 years. On the other hand, the government is doing all in its power to discourage the production of grain on the prairies. Any change in the Crow rate will be at the expense of the farmers, it appears, therefore affecting their net income. I do not know of a farmer who will voluntarily grow more grain with the knowledge that each new bushel that he grows will decrease his present net income. It is unfair to ask that of any sector in our economy. Even the Minister of Agriculture must realize that if he makes the farmers pay more to ship their grain he is undermining his whole strategy for increased exports, which we conceivably will not be able to get to the terminals.
I ask members to recognize the economic importance to all Canadians of the statutory Crow rate, which was locked in so
many years ago but which is still very relevant. It must not be used as an excuse for the erosion of Canada's transportation system.

Mr. Speaker, once more the House is considering Bill C-93, which authorizes the Canadian government to borrow money in order to meet its obligations for the fiscal year. Canadians probably wonder why Canada is borrowing money, what is going on and especially, why there seems to be some disagreement and debate about the fact that the Canadian government borrows money every year. A good question, because obviously, that money is being borrowed for a purpose. It is supposed to enable the government to meet its obligations to the people of this country. In fact, there is a vast complex of Canadian legislation that obliges the government to spend money, legislation brought in by the Liberal and Progressive Conservative governments, and passed in the House of Commons by Liberal, Progressive Conservative and NDP members, in other words by members of all parties.
So if all present members and their predecessors, who have worked in committee in the House of Commons in order to create laws with a view to better government and the wellbeing of all Canadians, if they passed these laws, they should know what they involve. So why do we always have a debate whenever the government has to borrow money? Why borrow money? I think that the member who is here to represent his constituency, who knows his job and knows the statutes, is not going to ask "why borrow money" at the end of the year. The Government of Canada has made commitments to the Canadian people and it must meet those commitments. Those commitments were made under legislation passed in this House, at the request of the Canadian people. So why should there be any attempt to have a debate on the question whether a government should or should not borrow? It is both necessary and normal that as a result of presentations or suggestions made by members of the House of Commons, by groups and by individual Canadians, that the government should borrow when its funds are not adequate to meet its commitments. And speaking of commitments, Mr. Speaker, it would perhaps be useful to define more clearly for the people across Canada and the people in our ridings what these obligations are.
Not long ago in Ottawa there was a first ministers' conference on the economy. The Government of Canada was told:
February 17, 1982

You are causing the problem, you are trying to fight inflation but you are not trying to fight unemployment, you are doing this and you are doing that. In fact, it was the same old story: blame everything on the federal government.
If we look at the facts, we must ask ourselves a few questions. Is the Canadian government really fighting unemployment? I shall take my riding as an example, Mr. Speaker. There are job-creation programs across Canada, and this year, the riding of Lac-Saint-Jean received its first grant of $1.5 million under the Community Development Program. Subsequent increases added $600,000 to that amount, which means that for the current year, Lac-Saint-Jean will receive $2.2 million under this program and I am not including the quarter million for the Opportunities for Youth program this summer, the vast number of policies being implemented by DREE, which is paying 25 per cent of capital investment in new projects, $5,000 per new job created, and so forth. The Canadian government is clearly spending money on job creation. The amounts involved may be fairly high for a single riding-$2 million-but we can certainly not accuse the government of not doing its job and not creating jobs. I challenge any province in Canada to come up with a plan that can compete with what the government is doing, and I would particularly challenge the government of the Province of Quebec, the PQ government, which is bragging about its own job-creation activities.
Last year, Mr. Speaker, 58,000 jobs were created in Quebec by the Canadian government, and whether or not they were temporary, at least people had work. And here is another way the Canadian government spends money in my riding: at the Canada Employment Centre in Alma, and I am not including the centre in Chicoutimi-my riding is so big that it has two centres-in Alma alone, 6,200 unemployed workers are registered with the centre and receive an average of $100 per week each in unemployment insurance benefits. This means that the Government of Canada has invested $600,000 per week in the Alma district, Mr. Speaker, which means $30 million annually. I challenge the government of the province of Quebec, the PQ government, to show me any figures that can disprove that.
Mr. Speaker, to use an example that brings the subject even closer to home and makes us realize what the Canadian government is doing for Canadians, take the average Canadian who gets up to go to work, and who happens to live in the Lac-Saint-Jean area. So everybody gets up in the morning, which is not unusual. You turn on the radio, and if you listen to the CBC, you may not realize this but its annual deficit costs the government $600 million, and the total cost is almost $1 billion. Then at breakfast, if you happen to like cheese or butter on your toast, these products are subsidized by the Canadian government to the tune of $2.60 per hundredweight of milk-$2.66 according to my colleague, the member for Roberval (Mrs. Beauchamp-Niquet), and she is right. After breakfast, our average Canadian may, if he is a man, use an
Taxation
electric razor, and in some provinces he will probably be using electric power generated by plants the Canadian government helped to set up-not in Quebec, however, where hydro is strictly a provincial matter.
Meanwhile, the heating system, which has been on all night and is on all day, runs on oil, and in eastern Canada this is imported oil which is almost 50 per cent subsidized by the Canadian government. When our average Canadian gets in his car, he may drive to a service station to buy gas with Canadian dollars which cost the government billions of dollars to keep at a reasonable level. The gas is subsidized by the Government of Canada by almost 50 per cent. And I can go on like this all day, merely listing areas where the Canadian government is involved in our daily lives, including recreation, cultural activities, nutrition and health. Because, you know, if that individual is a health or a social worker, 60 per cent of his salary is paid by the Government of Canada. If he works in a post-secondary school or at a university, if he is a support worker in some schools, 58 per cent of his salary is paid by the Government of Canada. We are then asked in the House, Mr. Speaker, why the government has to borrow. Quite simply in order to meet Canadian needs. I know that as far as the Progressive Conservative opposition is concerned, if the government borrowed to wage war, there would be no problem. That is a good idea. There would be no problem either if we wanted to give financial aid to the British government. It has been done in the past and such a move was applauded. However, if economic conditions become more difficult, as our young people seeking jobs have learned during the past ten years, and the government borrows billions to meet their needs, some find it strange. Questions are raised.
All the same, it should be realized, Mr. Speaker, that Canada is the second largest country in the world with only 24 million inhabitants. It is one of the countries endowed with the most resources in the world. Compare countries of equivalent size and their population: India with more than 600 million, China, one billion, Russia, 300 million, the United States, 250 million, Brazil 200 million. They have no more resources than we have. It will be suggested that we should perhaps restrict our social and job-creation policies or reduce our spending because we are only 24 million inhabitants with the greatest wealth for the future. No, Mr. Speaker, 1 think that this government should take action. The provincial governments are always asking us to do something and, what is more fantastic, so is the opposition, which blames us for borrowing. They urge us to create jobs and use the means at our disposal. One hon. member will say he has this or that project in his riding, another will say that he has such and such a project in his own riding, and so on and so forth. The requests keep on coming from both sides of the House. So I am amazed today when I see these same hon. members stand up in the House and say that the government should stop borrowing. I do not agree with them.

February 17, 1982

Mr. Speaker, if the government must intervene in these critical times for the economy, it is because year after year it has fought against high inflation and unemployment by increasing productivity. Canada's record between 1970 and 1980 was the best of all industrialized nations. In Canada, we are proud to be able to say that Canada has a better record than any other country on a job-population ratio. How is that? Because the Canadian government, under the leadership of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), is the government which developed the most projects and which helped put together programs for streamlining the industry. And this, in many ways. And because of this, our industry has not had the time to age. Today, we are having difficulties in a number of areas.
Let us consider the case of the automobile industry. That is an area where we are having difficulties. Why? Quite simply because we do not control this industry. It is clear that our automobile industry is an important element of the North American automobile industry as a whole, and if our industry is lacking in productivity, it is because we do not control enough of the factors to help it develop. And because of the slowing down of the whole automobile industry in North America, we must accept the lot we share with the Americans. But in other areas, Mr. Speaker, in the case for instance of Canadair, we have a fantastic and extraordinary record. My only qualm about the aeronautics industry is that around 1957 or 1958, it reduced its activities, although is was recognized as the best airplane builder in the world. This occurred unfortunately while a progressive government was in power, but we must still live with the consequences. However, a government rose in 1977 which was not afraid to invest money.
Of course, we had to borrow to invest in Canadair but today it has 6,000 people on its payroll as compared to 1,300 hardly four years ago. And now, Mr. Speaker, the case of Bombardier. Who asked the Bombardier company to manufacture something other than snowmobiles? Who asked them to manufacture buses, trains, subway cars and to go into the field of transportation? Who did? I see the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) has just awarded them a contract for trucks. Who has urged them to buy a licence to build jeeps? The Government of Canada has. That is where the government invests the billions of dollars it borrows. Fortunately, those billions of dollars have meant increased revenues for the government in recent years. What for? They have enabled the government to implement aid policies for ail Canadians in the field of health and education, and to help idle workers in trying situations. What about manpower training? Here again the government has been the driving force, the major motivation of Canadians to prosper, and above all it has given them the necessary tools. We are entering a new and important phase.
Right now, some of our basic industries such as the one I referred to earlier, the automobile industry, need revamping. Our industries updated their equipment ten years ago and now
find that they will have to go through the same process over again. They will have to rebuild and, in that respect, the Government of Canada is already on the move. Was it not the Canadian government that signed agreements with the provinces to modernize the pulp and paper mills and ensure reforestation? Indeed it was. We are building for the future. The $5 billion borrowing authority we are seeking today, those $6.6 billion are earmarked for that future. In what context?
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) is now negotiating new manpower training agreements with the provinces. We as Canadians-and 1 mean industrial workers as well as their representatives here or in any other legislature-we Canadians want to be able to continue saying that we are the best workers in the world, the most competent, the most productive, as it has always been our trademark. That is why this government is already spending hundreds of millions of dollars for manpower training. I need only refer to the Canada Manpower Industrial Training Program through which millions have been invested in the Lac-Saint-Jean riding. I need only refer to the new policies being implemented with respect to designated areas.
Let us see what has been going on in the regions of Sept-Iles, Tracy-Sorel, Drummondville and, lately, Montmag-ny. The Government of Canada took the initiative and decided to spend the funds required to retrain workers who are interested in new challenges and want to learn new skills. It also decided to spend money to help update those industries which could be modernized and to support others which could not face the challenge single handed. That is the role of a government. Mr. Speaker, why should the Government of Canada be afraid to borrow when necessary if any Canadian can do so when his needs exceed his capacity to pay? Why should the Government of Canada be expected to act differently than Canadians? Does the Government of Canada represent Russia or the Russian people? No! The Canadian government is like the Canadian people. It is vigorous, it knows its potential and it has confidence in the future. Indeed, to be able to borrow, one must have confidence in the future. And one of the resources of this country for the future is our youth. Of course, the Government of Canada could say tomorrow morning: We shall no longer pay for unemployment insurance. We need to borrow $6.6 billion, but instead, we shall stop paying the $4.8 billion deficit for unemployment insurance. Then, our borrowings would only amount to $1.8 billion instead of $6.6 billion. But what would become of our young people, Mr. Speaker? What about our major resource? What is unemployment insurance in the final analysis if not temporary support for someone with practical employment problems, if not the possibility for people to receive training during a period when they cannot find jobs. That is what it is!
If we were to abandon our young people tomorrow morning, what would become of them? They would do as others have

done. They would probably do what my father did when he left his native Lebanon, they would go to another country where they can get a job. We would then have lost part of our major resource. We might have saved 25 cents by refusing them unemployment insurance benefits, but it would have cost us thousands of dollars and the loss of an immeasurable human resource. If this is the type of policy that some want to implement in this country, let them do it. I can assure you that the end result will not be anything like the vision that a Liberal can have of our country.

Mr. Speaker, I know that the members opposite can only laugh. I have been a member of this House for over two years, and during that time 1 have seen those people laugh at Canadians regularly. They come here as teenagers, as 18-year-old children who only want to create a disturbance and are not interested in seeing Canada develop. 1 shall go even further. They form coalitions with certain provinces simply to play a political game. They are not interested in the development of Canadians, but simply in keeping their little constituencies, their little jobs as Members of Parliament. Not one of them would be willing tomorrow morning to risk his seat to help a youth in his own riding to develop. 1 know some members from Alberta and Saskatchewan who come here to complain that everything is wrong in Canada.
Go and see their provinces. Never before has the western economy been doing so well. Never! Thanks to whom? Certainly not to the nine months of Progressive Conservative rule! In nine months, the Progressive Conservatives moved the Canadian embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. In nine months, they almost went to war against Russia. Canadian sales abroad came to a stop. In nine months, they had time to sell Petro-Canada, scuttle Loto Canada and almost get rid of the CBC.
Mr. Speaker, it makes you wonder whether these people are Canadians. As a case in point, last year, when we wanted
Taxation
to call our national holiday Canada Day, they preferred the name Dominion Day. Anything that is called Canada bothers them. Whether it be Labour and Immigration Canada or Unemployment Insurance Canada, or Finance Canada. My impression is, they are much more interested in the development of their personal friends' corporations. And, Mr. Speaker, I seriously ask myself why opposition members come here in this House and ask the government: Why borrow $6.6 billion? The hon. gentlemen all know very well that this stems from legislation they themselves passed for the benefit of Canadians. All they have to do is allow the Government of Canada to go on helping Canadians. For instance, I recently heard the Quebec government referring to a salary for housewives at home. 1 would like to state, Mr. Speaker, that the only government doing something in that area is the Canadian government, through the child tax credit we are giving them each year, over and above family allowances. This is what the Canadian government is all about, the redistribution of wealth, notwithstanding the Progressive Conservatives and the opposition from the New Democratic Party, or should I say the New Salvadoran Party.
Mr. Speaker, I hope next year we will not have once more to face such an austere debate, to know what are the benefits Canadians derive from their own government. Why does this government work so hard for Canadians, their development in a climate where they will become the most developed citizens in the world, the most productive ones, to the benefit of our whole society and our future in particular, despite reactionary opposition members?
